newsitem.title: UK: Euro shares trim gains, dollar ends higher.
newsitem.headline: Euro shares trim gains, dollar ends higher.

text.p: European stock markets regained some ground on Friday after recent losses but ended below their highs as key U.S. data, while providing no shocks, reinforced expectations of higher interest rates.
Wall Street was down more than a percentage point at one stage, led by a drop in shares of computer giant IBM and weaker bonds, but recovered to show hardly any change by late morning in New York.
On the currency market, the dollar lost some of its buoyancy against the mark in late dealings, amid concern that weaker U.S. asset markets could undermine the U.S. currency.

But it remained up on the day after an early boost from U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, who calmed some fears over U.S.-Japan trade tensions, saying currencies should not be used as trade weapons.
Meanwhile, a sell-off by speculative funds hit various commodities such as silver and coffee and gold slid in silver's wake, losing $1.20 on the day at $347.45.

The U.S. central bank's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) boosted interest rates by a quarter point last week and markets had awaited Friday's jobs and earnings data for clues on whether it could raise rates again next month.

The March rise in U.S. non-farm payrolls was reported at 175,000, compared with economists' forecast of a 196,000 increase. The U.S. jobless rate edged down to 5.2 percent from 5.3 percent in February.
Average hourly earnings rose 0.4 percent -- in line with expectations but likely to cause concern over inflation.

"The figures are consistent with tight labour market conditions and consistent with another rate move at the May 20 FOMC meeting," said Neil MacKinnon, chief economist at Citibank in London. "I am going for another quarter point rise."
"The non-farm payroll is slightly below market expectations but the average hourly earnings increase of five cents underlines Fed worries about wage inflation."
The London stock market, Europe's biggest, ended with moderate gains as the Dow recovered from its early drop -- which followed falls in four of the five previous sessions.
But dealers said equity markets on both sides of the Atlantic remained vulnerable.

Despite earlier talk of European bourses decoupling from moves in New York, they said the British market was set to remain under Wall Street's spell as investors fret about rising U.S. rates and American first-quarter earnings reports.
"Pundits keep saying the market has discounted further U.S. rate hikes -- but it hasn't," the head of trading at a major London investment bank said.

In Frankfurt, where the bourse gained almost one percent in bourse floor trade, buying interest focused on the export-driven chemical and car industries lifted German shares. But dealers were wary about prospects after sharp recent losses.
"Monday is the earliest we will really be able to tell if we have found a real floor," said one Frankfurt dealer.
Showing fluctuating views in afternoon electronic trading, the Frankfurt market extended its gains, then rapidly fell back before ending roughly in the middle of the day's range.

French stocks also endured a roller-coaster ride, gaining around one percent, then dropping back to show losses before snapping a three-day losing streak with marginal gains. Paris traders said the U.S. jobs report contained contradictory elements.
Thomson-CSF fell 3.4 percent to 186.50 francs. The French government said Britain's General Electric was not eligible to bid for it. GEC was down 3-1/2 pence at 383.

In currencies, the dollar rose after Rubin, who had recently spooked it by warning Japan not to let its huge trade surplus swell again, repeated similar comments in Tokyo -- but rejected the notion that a stronger yen was the best way to act.
"We don't believe in anybody using their currency for trade policies -- us or anybody else," he told reporters.
"The comments (by Rubin) suggest the dollar is still in an uptrend and dollar/yen should go higher," said Stuart Frost, currency analyst at NatWest Markets.
Some analysts felt, however, that his message contained a veiled threat to Japan.
For those with a more long-range focus, European Union finance ministers arrived in the Netherlands for an informal meeting until Sunday to discuss economic and monetary union.
CURRENCIES AT THE EUROPEAN CLOSE
The dollar was quoted around 1.6768 marks and 124.23 yen, up from 1.6681 and 122.59 in late European trade on Thursday. Its day's high against the mark was 1.6795.
STOCK MARKETS AT THE EUROPEAN CLOSE
LONDON - The FTSE-100 index ended up 22.0 points or 0.52 percent at 4,236.6 after a high of 4,247.6.
PARIS - The CAC-40 closed up 3.45 points or 0.14 percent to 2,517.97, well below an earlier peak of 2,541.73 but above a mid-afternoon low of 2,498.72.
FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index ended bourse floor trade up 29.69 points or 0.92 percent at 3,244.93. The IBIS DAX in later electronic trade hit a high of 3,262.13 before ending at 3,235.35.
PRECIOUS METALS AT THE EUROPEAN CLOSE
Gold ended London trading around $347.45, paring earlier losses as pressure on silver eased but still below the previous close of $348.65. Silver slipped to $4.73 from $4.83.
